teaser: The clients refused it, the critics called it a snowman, and Rodin took it home.
review_notes:
The photo shows a bronze cast with a green patina in a park, with a label at the base; it is not the Musée Rodin cast (probably the Middelheim Museum, Antwerp). The work is the same.
Fee of 10,000 francs returned by Rodin: check amount.
Insults quoted (snowman, sack of plaster, seal, penguin) are the ones usually reported from the 1898 press.
Story of Rodin ordering clothes from Balzac's former tailor: widely reported, check.
Dressing gown dipped in plaster for the drapery study: check.
First bronze installed in Paris in 1939 at the crossing of boulevards Raspail and Montparnasse.
Steichen's moonlight photographs dated 1908.
Height about 2.7 m.

lesson.text: Paris, spring 1898. A tall white plaster goes on show at the Salon, the big yearly art exhibition. The writers' society that ordered it, and waited seven years for it, studies the thing and issues a statement: it refuses to recognize this as a statue of Balzac. The order is given to someone else.

Honoré de Balzac had died in 1850, leaving close to a hundred novels and stories about French society. In 1891 the Société des Gens de Lettres, then led by the novelist Émile Zola, asked Auguste Rodin for a monument. He promised it in eighteen months.

Rodin never met Balzac, so he investigated like a detective. He traveled to the writer's home region to study local faces, and he is said to have tracked down Balzac's old tailor to order a suit cut to the dead man's measurements.

The measurements described a short, heavy man with a big belly. Rodin modeled him naked first, arms crossed, planted like a wrestler. Then he remembered a habit: Balzac wrote through the night in a loose robe, like a monk's. Rodin wrapped his figure in it, and the body disappeared.

lesson.title: What is left of a man
lesson.text: Under the robe, Rodin kept only three or four signs of the person.

spots.title: The head
spots.text: Thrown back, with a mane of hair and eyes sunk into two dark hollows. The features are roughed in more than drawn. From far away they read as one expression: defiance.

spots.title: The collar
spots.text: The lapels of the robe open like a funnel, and the thick neck rises out of it. The whole statue works as a pedestal for the head.

spots.title: The empty sleeve
spots.text: This sleeve hangs flat. No arm is in it. Balzac wears his robe thrown over the shoulders like a cape, which turns the body into a single block.

lesson.text: No hands on show, no pen, no book, no chair. A monument to a writer normally lists such things, so that passers-by know who is being honored and why. Rodin removed every one of them. What he wanted to show was not Balzac's job but the force of a mind at work.
Rodin's Balzac is a portrait of an inner state rather than of a person's looks. That shift, from likeness to feeling, is one of the doors modern sculpture walked through.

The press had a field day in 1898. The statue was compared to a snowman, a sack of plaster, a seal and a penguin. Friends of Rodin, including the painter Claude Monet, signed a letter of support and offered to buy it.

Rodin turned down the offers. He gave the society its money back and carted the plaster to his house in Meudon, outside Paris. He said it would never leave him, and he was right: no bronze was cast while he lived.
What exactly bothered people? Partly the rough surface. Mostly the shape. A proper statue stands straight on its base. This one does something else, and you can trace it.
Follow the outline rather than the details.

lines.label: The lean
lines.text: From the feet to the head, the figure tilts backward. He seems to pull away from us and look over our heads, like someone rearing up.

lines.label: One block
lines.text: The silhouette is a single tapering mass, closer to a standing stone than to a human body. Critics saw a shapeless lump. Later sculptors saw the future.

lines.label: The long folds
lines.text: The folds fall in a few long strokes from the shoulder to the ground. They hurry your eye upward to the face, the only place where it can rest.

lesson.text: Ten years after the scandal, a young American photographer, Edward Steichen, spent nights in the Meudon garden shooting the plaster by moonlight. In his pictures it is a dark shape against the sky, nothing more. Rodin loved them. They showed the statue as he had meant it: as a silhouette.

Balzac finally got his Paris street corner in 1939, more than twenty years after Rodin died and forty-one after the rejection. A bronze was set up where two boulevards cross in Montparnasse, and it is still there.
The cast in this photo stands outdoors, as casts in several countries do, and weather has turned the bronze green. One question remains. If the sleeve is empty, where are the arms?
Balzac's hands are hidden. Tap the place where you think he is holding his robe shut from the inside.

spots.title: Under the cloth
spots.text: A swelling in the middle of the robe, where the two edges cross. In the nude studies the arms were folded right here. Rodin kept the gesture and buried it.

lesson.text: So the wrestler with crossed arms is still in there. Rodin spent seven years building a body he then chose to hide, and the hiding is the statue. The writers' society wanted a man in a coat. It was handed a rock with a face, and it took the world a few decades to see why that was better.

quiz.question: How did the writers' society react to the statue in 1898?
options: It refused to recognize it as Balzac
It asked for a larger version
quiz.explanation: The society rejected the plaster and gave the order to another sculptor.

quiz.question: Why is Balzac wrapped in a robe?
options: He wrote at night in a loose robe like a monk's
Rodin ran out of time to sculpt the body
The society demanded a clothed figure
quiz.explanation: Rodin used the writer's night-time working habit to turn the body into one block.

quiz.question: What did Rodin do after the rejection?
options: He sold it to Claude Monet
He returned the money and kept the plaster at Meudon
quiz.explanation: He refused all offers and kept the statue at home for the rest of his life.

quiz.question: What did Edward Steichen's photographs show?
options: The statue by moonlight, as a dark silhouette
quiz.explanation: Steichen photographed the plaster at night in the Meudon garden.

quiz.question: When was a bronze of the monument finally installed in Paris?
quiz.explanation: It went up in Montparnasse in 1939, long after Rodin's death.

facts.text: Rodin first modeled Balzac naked, with crossed arms, before covering him with a robe.
facts.explanation: The nude studies came first, and the folded arms are still hidden under the cloth.

facts.text: Balzac holds a pen and a book so that passers-by can identify him.
facts.explanation: Rodin removed every such attribute. Not even the hands are visible.

facts.text: Rodin delivered the monument in the eighteen months he had promised.
facts.explanation: It took him seven years, from 1891 to 1898.
